questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I chose a place that would be most beneficial for me in regards to my study. Keeping my studies in mind, I thought about what I wanted to gain from my exchange, would it be work-wise, language-wise, or other aspects, and then choose accordingly.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I would rate the overall study abroad experience between 8-9. I learned a lot from my stay, but due to covid-19 implications, some opportunities were limited such as campus life. Other than that I am happy I studied abroad.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Depending on what you need to know, the information is easy to find. The embassy of the desired country typically has a checklist for important notices to know before leaving, and in my case, our host university sent an email with further instructions. I would advise always double-checking before leaving, so nothing comes as a shock.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I got assistance from the host university's OIA (Office of International Affairs) and they helped me with any trouble during my whole stay. I also received assistance from the airport when leaving the airport and departing from it.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: The host University did a satisfactory job with the orientation and assistance for students.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Dormitory, in which you would share with another student/exchange student. Guesthouse.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: There were two options for meal plans. Plan A offers 60% of the total number of meals and Plan B offers 85% of the total number of meals. However, the meal plans only include breakfast and dinner. At the guesthouse, you had your own room with a kitchen.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Be sure to check what you need before leaving, so you don't have to purchase stuff upon arriving. The first month might be overwhelming with a roommate at a different country, and most likely with another exchange student that is not a fellow classmate, but you form a great companionship with them. Depending on what kind of room you get, the rooms might be to the small side.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The housing was okay.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was easy.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You receive an email from the OIA about when the online course registration will be held. In this time period, you are able to register for courses on a first-come-first-served basis, so it is best to start as soon as possible if you want specific courses. The course registration in itself was easy, you follow the link sent to you in the mail, and you press select the desired course on the course list then you are all settled. If the course is full you cannot select it. The registration process was held two times, the second wave was for those who missed the time period, but the courses available would be limited. You can also contact the professor of the desired course if you can join, but you would get approval from the OIA at first.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: It is possible to contact the OIA for questions.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got what I wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Be sure to check out the course descriptions before the registration process, so you know what courses you want. As the registration is on a first-come-first-served basis, it will be wise for you to add courses as early as the registration period begins. Additionally, be sure to check the timezone, so you don't mix up the time.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Very satisfied.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: My language program was fitted to accommodate my level, so I would improve. You take the placement test, and you strive to surpass it so you can study next level when you're done. The academic courses at the university were also great, it was reflective and fit the expectations.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Language program was very different and it was difficult at first to adapt, but once you get used to it, it was a good style flow. It was intense, but you improve a lot. The other course was similar to that of UCPH with a professor teaching and students taking notes and studying at home. As it was online, the teaching style was that of UCPH with zoom and PowerPoint with active debates or questions.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: PSYCHOLOGY OF RELIGION and Korean Language for Academic Purposes (KAP200)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend Psychology of Religion and KAP200 for future exchange students as they're very giving courses for academic purposes and insight. Psychology of Religion requires a philosophical approach, but it is available for all levels, and you don't need to be a psychology or religion major to follow it. The course highlights comprehensive thinking and debunking the fundamental problem with academic research focuses. The KAP200 is a very giving course if you want to improve your language skills with intense study. The course itself is intense and time-consuming, but time flies really fast and you get surprised with how much you've accomplished on a little time.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I did not realise I had nothing at the room upon arrival, so I had to buy blankets, pillows etc. Furthermore, as I had trouble with my SIMCARD not being able to call Denmark, I had to use my own SIMCARD and pay a lot. I would advise to get a simcard before leaving or make sure to get one on the day of arrival.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Books were very cheap. One school-book was almost the same as two at home. Eating out were also on the cheaper side as you most times get side dishes for free, so I ate out a lot. Getting a transportation card were convenient, and compared to Denmark way cheaper.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Did not get to enjoy it due to COVID-19, but what I did get to try I was very satisfied with!

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Buddy-group. You can sign up to get a buddy, and you can experience things together while language exchanging. HUG (another buddy organisation) prepare for social activities if you sign up for the facebook group.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Going hiking or experiencing temples! It is refreshing and beautiful to experience nature and culture on another level than reading it. I would recommend going to the less famous ones and visiting small coffee shops as the locals are very welcoming.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: I would recommend visiting the war museum, which has a lot of history and stories to tell. The entrance is free and you walk through a time-period from the first wars in Korea to the Korean War etc. At the museum they have different 'departments' with themes, so it is worth a visit.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: At first a bit challenging, but once you get used to it, it is alright. The food is delicious and if you find it difficult to communicate, you can use body language or just point with your fingers on the menu etc. You pick up on the local culture fast and you don't have to be afraid to make mistakes, as they will help you.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Be open and straightforward. A lot of people are shy to talk, but if you ask them for help or guidance, they will do a lot to help you. People often sat together outside the campus' convenience store, so that is a good place to start if you are shy.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: When eating out, you often have to call for the waiter to come instead of waiting as we do at home. In a lot of places you call out 'here' or 'excuse me' to let them know you are prepared to order, want more etc. as the waiters will help attend other customers or kitchen instead of waiting for you.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: If they see you struggle with something, they try to help you. I experienced a lot of kindness and strangers were curious and wanted to talk with me if the context allowed them to. I found it nice to talk with strangers and ask them for tips or recommendations.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Remember to take breaks, avoid talking in your native language or English even if its difficult, and join activities made by the university or its students. It is easy to be tempted to switch to english when you are out with new friends or when ordering etc, but you learn a lot from experience. If you cannot remember a word, try to describe it (with body language even) or guess it, the locals will either ask you or try to help you. As the study process is different from home and can feel heavy, it is important to take breaks and enjoy your time. Maybe try to study with some fellow classmates.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: I don't think so.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Experiencing the culture and trying new things while learning. I tried not to let my (sometimes) limited language stop me from being curious and tried to keep talking, asking questions, and expressing what I felt, which meant I got to talk to a lot of different people with different purposes.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Not preparing enough. I was very late in regards to making plans, buying SIMCARDS, etc. so it was a hectic first month for me to find out what I needed in a new country I had never been in before.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Going on an exchange does not only benefit you academically but also physically and socially. You learn a lot about culture and experience the language, culture, people, and student life on another level than what you read about. As cliche as it sounds, you grow a lot in character as you have to adapt to another lifestyle than the one you are used to. I would recommend studying abroad to improve a lot and to see the world from another perspective than from home.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
